statements.text: China has already, for example, put in place requirements for their A.I. models to not create A.I. bots or chatbots that would form personal relationships with children and young people. Don't our kids deserve the same? China has already put regulations on not having these A.I. tools create what's called deepfakes, false images of people. Shouldn't Americans have that same protection? And I think you can go ahead and put a bit of safety into this process and not lose the race.
I don't believe imminent existential threat, but potentially catastrophic threat, yes.
Short term, next three to five years, the economic disruption is going to be — I just think we are not ready at all.
I think, Nick, we need to do is set a federal baseline, and I think that means a data center of any size needs to come and bring their own power. They need to bring their own water.

we have already seen data into these large language models—everybody is talking about ChatGPT, but there is the ability to have these algorithms literally discriminate against consumers in the financial services sector.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the CFPB's Semiannual Report, where Senator Warner pivots from financial-regulation topics to AI risks and asks the CFPB Director about algorithmic discrimination.

statements.text: I want to move quickly to AI. I concur with Senator Cortez Masto on some of the questions she raised and Senator Menendez. I am chair of the Intelligence Committee, and I see upside, but I see huge, huge, downside. [...] How—in the minute and 30 seconds you have got left, how are you thinking about making sure that our public markets and the trust in those markets are not undermined by the rise of AI across the board?
statements.context: Senate Banking Committee oversight hearing on the SEC, where Senator Warner questions the SEC Chair about AI threats to public markets.

statements.text: And do we need to overweigh the risk because somebody giving a false tip could manipulate the market. But the volume of tools that could be used to mess with the market using these AI tools seems to me to be of a—what's the analogy—but the gas versus bullets, but there's something in—.
statements.context: Chairman Warner speaking during an open Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on the national security implications of AI.

statements.text: And I'm not saying from Dr. LeCun—but I have heard this from many: Oh gosh, you're going to regulate away innovation; you're going to kill the golden goose!
statements.context: Closing remarks by Chairman Warner at a Senate Select Committee on Intelligence hearing on AI and national security, responding to expert testimony.

statements.text: How do we democratize access with AI tools and yet still put some level of guardrails? And obviously, bearing in mind what Senator Rubio said, is you don't want to act and unilaterally disarm, but the notion of not putting some guardrails in place in a field that's changing so quickly.
statements.context: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence hearing on AI national security implications; Chairman Warner questioning Dr. Yann LeCun.

statements.text: I would respectfully say, I think the two most immediate potential harms with AI tools that have already been released is the ability for massive undermining of trust in our elections and massive underlying of trust in our public markets.
statements.context: Opening exchange in a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on the national-security implications of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: I'm really concerned that we've already seen, say with ChatGPT, that with very little push and pull, all of the guardrails of protections that were put in place didn't stand the test and you were very quickly starting to have a ChatGPT model give out answers that were way beyond its scope. [...] should we simply trust the vendors alone to make these determinations?
statements.context: Chairman Warner presides over an open Senate Select Committee on Intelligence hearing on AI and national security, questioning expert witnesses about vendor self-testing and AI alignment risks.

statements.text: But the volume of things that could take place from deep fakes to product misrepresentation to false SEC claims, just the litany—. Because I would argue that there was an overweighed risk of AI taking something that's already wrong and doing it on steroids exponentially. [...] does it need a new law? Does it need a lower standard of proof because the damage could be so great? Is it a higher penalty?
statements.context: Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on AI and national security, where Chairman Warner questions witnesses about regulatory responses to AI-amplified manipulation of elections and financial markets.

statements.text: And to the question, are not the AI tools ability to do that at scale so much greater than a traditional individual market manipulator of even 5 years ago?
statements.context: Senator Warner speaks during a hearing or discussion on Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services.

statements.text: I would argue that the two domains that completely rely on public trust, that where AI could be hugely manipulative, are faith in our elections and the tools that were used in 2016 are child's play based upon what deepfakes and other tools could be used on an effort on steroids.
statements.context: Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services, where Senator Warner questions panelists about AI threats to public markets and potential legislative responses.

statements.text: As I think about the exponentially greater power of AI in misinformation, disinformation, the level of bot usage, it is child's play to what happened in terms of Russia's 2016 interference, the tools that are existing now. I think it would be naive to underestimate that that we are dealing with a threat of a different magnitude.
statements.context: Senator Warner speaks at a Senate hearing titled "AI and the Future of Our Elections," addressing AI-driven disinformation, election interference, and market manipulation risks.

statements.text: I am extraordinarily concerned that AI could lead to massive market manipulation now.
statements.context: Senator Warner makes a closing remark during a Senate Banking Committee oversight hearing on financial regulators, suggesting FSOC should address AI-driven market manipulation risks.

statements.text: I want to raise an issue I do not believe has been raised today, and that is how you are thinking about artificial intelligence.
statements.context: Senate Banking Committee hearing on the CFPB's Semiannual Report to Congress, where Senator Warner questions the CFPB Director about AI risks.

statements.text: How are you thinking about framing any sense of guardrails around AI as we think about public trust in the public markets?
statements.context: Senate hearing on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Semiannual Report to Congress, where a senator questions the agency director.

statements.text: you could have some of these AI tools that someone could hide and say, I had no intent; I simply told the tool [...]
statements.context: Senator Warner speaking at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Semiannual Report to Congress.

statements.text: Where I have talked with lots of Members on this Committee are two areas where AI, not in terms of next generation but in today's generation tools could have dramatic effect in undermining public confidence. [...] And candidly, I have been surprised that we have not seen more massive use of AI tools, beyond kind of the fake tools, to manipulate our markets.
statements.context: Senator Warner speaks during the CFPB Director's Semiannual Report to Congress hearing, discussing AI's potential to undermine public confidence in elections and financial markets.

statements.text: Artificial intelligence, I know, has been touched. I personally am surprised that there was not greater concern about AI in terms of using its ability to disrupt faith in the public markets.
statements.context: Senate Banking Committee annual oversight hearing with Wall Street firm leaders.

statements.text: I have worked with Senator Kennedy on this Committee on a bill, Senate Bill 3554, the Financial Artificial Intelligence Risk Reduction Act, that goes after some of the challenges around AI in the financial markets where I think we have huge, huge vulnerabilities.
statements.context: Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on national security challenges and outpacing China in emerging technology.

statements.text: And one of the things that really concerns me is a lot of these AI tools, you may say just go make the most money possible, and that may then result in screwing around with consumers.
statements.context: Senate Banking Committee hearing on scams and fraud in the banking system, where Senator Warner pivoted from fraud and real-time reporting to AI-related risks.

statements.text: There is a whole new way around AI tools, with prompt inquiry and others, that do not really fit neatly into the bucket of cyber, but there are ways that we can manipulate these models in a huge way. I would welcome your input on how we do that.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in health care where Senator Warner pivots to national-security cyber concerns and solicits expert feedback on governing AI model manipulation.

statements.text: I just want to talk to that a little bit more, in terms of how we deal with this automation bias.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in healthcare where Senator Warner questions a witness about automation bias and liability.

statements.text: I just want to say one of the things I think we have to grapple with as well is intent, you know? I sit on the Banking Committee, where we are seeing AI tools that might have this notion of ``go make money,'' but then use illicit or illegal ways to do that. [...] Dr. Sendak, I want to start with you. I am very interested in your work on developing model disclosures for AI. But I worry—I was a tech guy 20 years before I got into this business—that there is such a first-mover advantage, and if we do not get that disclosure form right—and I know you have talked about using even maybe the nutrition guide tools.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in healthcare where Senator Warner questions a witness about model disclosure frameworks and AI intent issues.

statements.text: I would add, ladies and gentlemen, that at the Munich Security Conference, something I participated in, there were 20 tech companies that came together, most of the social media companies, on a voluntary basis to indicate both watermarking and willingness to take down AI-generated video and voice that were affecting elections, but it was voluntary, and the proof will be in the pudding.
statements.context: Remarks by Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Warner during the open hearing on the 2024 Worldwide Threats Assessment.

statements.text: Artificial intelligence can accelerate software development but can also accelerate malicious cyber attacks or the spread of misinformation.
statements.context: Opening statement by the Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman at the annual Worldwide Threats Assessment hearing.

statements.text: S. 4230. A bill to improve the tracking and processing of security and safety incidents and risks associated with artificial intelligence, and for other purposes; to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
statements.context: Introduction of bills on the Senate floor during routine morning business.

statements.text: Lots and lots of talk about AI. There's not a week that goes by that we don't see a new enhancement in terms of either video or audio deepfake capabilities. I don't think, even though we passed some bipartisan legislation out of the Rules Committee today, that will get the national legislation on deepfakes. [...] And those of us who have been pushing the tech companies to do more—there were 20 tech companies that came together in what was called the Munich Accord. [...] promising that they would have a commonality of watermarking, so you can indicate if something has been altered, this AI in elections, a commitment to try to take that content down and to educate voters. [...] I worry that after that much publicized announcement in February to use the old political term—``where's the beef?''—I don't see that common watermarking standard emerging.
statements.context: Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on foreign threats to the 2024 elections, where Chairman Warner questioned agency directors about AI deepfake risks and tech-company collaboration.

statements.text: relevant emerging technologies, particularly generative AI and big data analytics, are increasing the threat by enabling the proliferation of influence actors who can conduct targeted campaigns, reducing the number of relatively sophisticated influence operations and content, and further complicating attribution. For example, innovations in AI have enabled foreign influence actors to produce seemingly authentic and tailored messaging more eficiently at greater scale and with content adapted for different languages and cultures.
statements.context: Senate Intelligence Committee open hearing on foreign threats to the 2024 U.S. elections.

statements.text: the scale and sophistication of these sorts of attacks against our elections can now be accelerated by AI tools. The truth is the kind of audio and video manipulation that even as recently as four years ago and clearly eight years ago was still a challenge now can happen at a speed and scale due to AI tools that's unprecedented. [...] I fear that Congress's inability to pass any new guardrails in the last 18 months for AI-enabled mischief really could pose a huge problem.
statements.context: Opening statement at a Senate Intelligence Committee open hearing on foreign threats to the 2024 U.S. elections.

statements.text: I do want to, though, compliment the fact that Senator Kennedy and I both have been, I think, trying to figure out how we grapple with AI. [...] We introduced the Financial Artificial Intelligence Risk Reduction, FAIRR Act.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the CFPB's Semiannual Report to Congress, where Senator Warner discusses his AI-focused financial legislation and questions the CFPB Director.

statements.text: I would be amazed if we don't subsequently find out that, maybe not Fortune 100 companies but Fortune 100 to 500 companies, that there is a lot of manipulation going on here.
statements.context: Senator Warner speaks during a congressional session reviewing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Semiannual Report, discussing AI-driven market manipulation and election interference.

statements.text: Because, you know, just as deepfakes can manipulate our political process, you know, you could see AI tools at scale and speed manipulate our history and cultural in ways that could be frankly devastating.
statements.context: Senator Warner raises AI concerns during a Smithsonian Institution oversight hearing, asking the witness about protecting collections from AI manipulation.

statements.text: I have got a half a dozen bipartisan AI laws or bills, some of them addressing things like how we avoid those entities that circumvent the watermarks that you and others may put in.
statements.context: Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Warner closes a hearing on foreign threats to the 2024 election, addressing executives from U.S. technology companies.

statements.text: As we have seen just over the last two years, AI technology is rapidly evolving in a way that will have massive consequences for our economy, national security, and even democracy. I am heartened to see the administration recognize this very fact and take a leadership role to advance AI capabilities while simultaneously promoting responsible research, strong governance that ensures trust and safety, and the protection of human and civil rights.
statements.venue: Press release statement on Biden AI National Security Memorandum

statements.text: If there was ever a topic that seemed to be made for an FSOC type review, it would be AI and the ability to have AI manipulate the public markets.
statements.context: Senate hearing on consumer protection and workers' financial security, where Senator Warner questions a witness about AI-driven financial market manipulation and FSOC oversight.

statements.text: Well, why sell some of our most cutting edge chips to China? It is a complete contradiction in in policy.

What I am more worried about than the recent announcements, the 15,000 or 14,000 job losses at the big tech companies, is the job dislocation that takes place in terms of jobs not being created in the first place. [...] Many big banks have shared with me they are cutting interns and first-year hires in half, and planning to do so next year too.
Communities should not be asked to shoulder the costs of the AI revolution without knowing what they’re signing up for
statements.venue: Senate floor speech, quoted in The Alexandria Brief

statements.text: But we also know that there's a number of AI tools that still have a tendency to hallucinate and, um, with that tendency, sometimes it poses major security risks.
statements.context: Senate Armed Services Committee open hearing on the nomination of Lt. General Joshua Rudd to be NSA Director.

statements.text: I will bet anybody in the audience that goes to 30 or 35% within the next two years [...] And if we don’t figure this out—I say this as a pro-AI, pro-tech guy—we’re going to get screwed.
A data center moratorium simply means China is gonna move quicker, and this is one where we can’t lose.
I think we’re going to need a pretty radical transformation. And if we simply do a traditional government training program, we’re going to screw it up.

I salute the proposal for pre-deployment testing on a collaborative basis – just as I did when that idea was first advanced in the last administration’s EO, which was rescinded on Trump’s first day. I am strongly supportive of the effort to have NSA lead efforts to evaluate national security implications of frontier models in voluntary partnerships with frontier vendors – which is why we’ve included a provision directing NSA to do that in each of the last three years’ Intelligence Authorization bills my Committee has passed – which had been rebuffed by Trump allies in 2024 and 2025.
statements.venue: Press release statement on Trump's AI executive order

statements.text: S. 5047. A bill to require the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology to establish a working group to facilitate coordination among relevant stakeholders regarding compound risks relating to artificial intelligence physical systems [...] S. 5054. A bill to exempt AI data centers from bonus depreciation and require data center operators to submit certain information relating to electricity and water use [...] S. 5057. A bill to prohibit the use of certain artificial intelligence models across the Federal Government [...] S. 5061. A bill to improve the tracking and processing of security and safety incidents and risks associated with artificial intelligence [...]
statements.context: Senate floor introduction of bills and joint resolutions, with multiple AI-related bills introduced by Senator Warner and others.

statements.text: I share the concern of many Americans that the impacts of this technology on our country and on our culture could also, if we don't get it right, be catastrophic. [...] That is why today I am introducing a legislative agenda—a series of bills—built around four simple principles: [...] we need meaningful safeguards against abuse. [...] Finally, I want to talk about artificial intelligence through the lens of national security.
statements.context: Senate floor remarks introducing a multi-bill AI legislative agenda during Executive Calendar proceedings.

statements.text: The same frontier AI models that accelerate discovery can also figure out where the vulnerabilities are in our systems. [...] The most advanced AI systems deserve a higher standard of security before they are widely deployed.
statements.context: Senator Mark Warner speaks on the Senate floor advocating for AI security legislation during an Executive Calendar session.

statements.text: Today, unemployment among recent college graduates has risen to levels that should concern all of us. Many of the occupations most vulnerable to generative AI are the very white-collar, entry-level jobs that have long served as the first rung on the career ladder – jobs in business, finance, marketing, software development, customer support, and other knowledge professions.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI agenda

statements.text: Right now, the honest answer is that we don’t know nearly enough. Congress has remarkably little visibility into how AI is affecting hiring, wages, productivity, or job displacement across the economy. We’re debating one of the most consequential technological transformations in history with surprisingly little real-time data.
statements.venue: Senate floor speech on AI agenda

statements.text: Artificial intelligence is one of the defining national security challenges of our time, and I welcome the administration recognizing that this technology requires serious, sustained attention at the highest levels of government. But creating a new title is not a substitute for having a coherent strategy. So far, the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
statements.venue: Press release statement on Jay Clayton's appointment to coordinate AI policy
